items.stem: Define the term "disinflation".
items.answer: A fall in the rate of inflation, while prices are still rising
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a fall in the rate of inflation, while prices are still rising. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Ana writes: "If inflation falls from 6% to 3%, prices are falling." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Prices are still rising, but more slowly (disinflation). Prices fall only with negative inflation (deflation).
items.markingKey: Prices are still rising, but more slowly (disinflation). Prices fall only with negative inflation (deflation). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why different households experience different rates of inflation.
items.answer: Their spending patterns differ: low-income households spend a larger share on food and energy, so when those prices rise quickly, their personal inflation rate exceeds the CPI average. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Their spending patterns differ: low-income households spend a larger share on food and energy, so when those prices rise quickly, their personal inflation rate exceeds the CPI average. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "A 10% rise in the price of petrol means the inflation rate rises by 10%." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Petrol has a small weight in the CPI; if its weight is 4%, it adds only about 0.4 percentage points to inflation.
items.markingKey: Petrol has a small weight in the CPI; if its weight is 4%, it adds only about 0.4 percentage points to inflation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a 10% rise in the price of petrol means the inflation rate rises by 10%. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Petrol has a small weight in the CPI; if its weight is 4%, it adds only about 0.4 percentage points to inflation.
items.markingKey: Petrol has a small weight in the CPI; if its weight is 4%, it adds only about 0.4 percentage points to inflation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kalimar's central bank reports annual CPI inflation of 2% followed by 10%. Taking the CPI as 100 at the start of year 1, calculate the CPI at the end of year 2 and the total percentage increase in the price level.
items.markingKey: 100 × (1 + 2/100) × (1 + 10/100) = 112.2. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for 12.2%. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The consumer price index is an accurate measure of changes in the cost of living."
items.answer: It is a reasonable measure of average price changes, but it is less accurate for specific groups and during rapid structural change.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: based on large, regular price surveys; weights updated with expenditure surveys; internationally comparable methodology. Arguments against: substitution, quality and new-product biases; average household may not represent any real household; excludes or poorly measures housing costs in some countries; informal markets omitted. Supported judgement: It is a reasonable measure of average price changes, but it is less accurate for specific groups and during rapid structural change.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "producer price index (PPI)"?
options: Extremely rapid inflation, often defined as more than 50% a month
The main goals of macroeconomic policy: economic growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation, a sustainable balance of payments and an equitable distribution of income
The costs to firms of frequently changing prices, such as reprinting price lists and updating systems
An index of the prices of inputs and outputs of producers, often a leading indicator of consumer price inflation
items.answer: An index of the prices of inputs and outputs of producers, often a leading indicator of consumer price inflation
items.markingKey: D. "producer price index (PPI)" is an index of the prices of inputs and outputs of producers, often a leading indicator of consumer price inflation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the CPI may overstate the true rise in the cost of living.
items.answer: It uses a fixed basket, so it ignores consumers switching to cheaper substitutes, improvements in quality and the introduction of new products, all of which reduce the effective cost of living.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It uses a fixed basket, so it ignores consumers switching to cheaper substitutes, improvements in quality and the introduction of new products, all of which reduce the effective cost of living. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a weighted price index is used rather than a simple average of price changes.
items.answer: Households spend different shares of income on different goods; a 10% rise in rent matters more than a 10% rise in the price of salt, so weights by expenditure share reflect the impact on the cost of living.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Households spend different shares of income on different goods; a 10% rise in rent matters more than a 10% rise in the price of salt, so weights by expenditure share reflect the impact on the cost of living. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using UK CPI inflation in 2022 as an example, explain limitations of the CPI.
items.answer: UK CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022, driven by energy and food prices; lower-income households, who spend more on these items, faced higher personal inflation rates. A single average rate hid the much larger rise in the cost of living for low-income households
items.markingKey: Context (UK CPI inflation peaked at 11.1% in October 2022, driven by energy and food prices; lower-income households, who spend more on these items, faced higher personal inflation rates.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A single average rate hid the much larger rise in the cost of living for low-income households – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to limitations of the CPI.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "cost-push inflation"?
options: A fall in the rate of inflation, while prices are still rising
Inflation caused by increases in costs of production, such as wages, energy or imported raw materials, which shift SRAS to the left
A situation where achieving one macroeconomic objective makes achieving another more difficult
Inflation measured excluding volatile items such as food and energy prices
items.answer: Inflation caused by increases in costs of production, such as wages, energy or imported raw materials, which shift SRAS to the left
items.markingKey: B. "cost-push inflation" is inflation caused by increases in costs of production, such as wages, energy or imported raw materials, which shift SRAS to the left.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Inflation always harms everyone equally." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Inflation redistributes: borrowers with fixed-rate debt gain, while savers, lenders and people on fixed incomes lose.
items.markingKey: Inflation redistributes: borrowers with fixed-rate debt gain, while savers, lenders and people on fixed incomes lose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Deflation is always good because goods become cheaper." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Good deflation from productivity gains can be benign, but demand-led deflation reduces spending, raises real debt burdens and can deepen recessions.
items.markingKey: Good deflation from productivity gains can be benign, but demand-led deflation reduces spending, raises real debt burdens and can deepen recessions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Zimbabwe's hyperinflation and explain what it reveals about consequences of very high inflation.
items.answer: Zimbabwe's monthly inflation was estimated at about 79.6 billion per cent in November 2008, after rapid money printing to finance government spending; the country abandoned its currency in 2009. Money ceased to be a store of value or medium of exchange, savings were wiped out and the economy dollarised
items.markingKey: Context (Zimbabwe's monthly inflation was estimated at about 79.6 billion per cent in November 2008, after rapid money printing to finance government spending; the country abandoned its currency in 2009.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Money ceased to be a store of value or medium of exchange, savings were wiped out and the economy dollarised – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to consequences of very high inflation.

items.stem: Briefly describe energy-driven inflation in the euro area in 2022 and explain what it reveals about cost-push inflation.
items.answer: Euro-area inflation reached 10.6% in October 2022, with energy prices up over 40% year on year. Higher energy costs shifted SRAS left, raising prices while growth slowed
items.markingKey: Context (Euro-area inflation reached 10.6% in October 2022, with energy prices up over 40% year on year.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Higher energy costs shifted SRAS left, raising prices while growth slowed – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cost-push inflation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Japan's deflation and explain what it reveals about consequences of deflation.
items.answer: Japan experienced falling or flat consumer prices for much of 1998-2012, with weak growth and very low interest rates. Expectations of falling prices reduced spending and investment, and real debt burdens rose
items.markingKey: Context (Japan experienced falling or flat consumer prices for much of 1998-2012, with weak growth and very low interest rates.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Expectations of falling prices reduced spending and investment, and real debt burdens rose – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to consequences of deflation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that deflation is more harmful to an economy than inflation.
items.answer: Persistent demand-led deflation is usually more damaging than moderate inflation, which is why central banks target low positive inflation of about 2%.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: deflationary spiral reduces AD and output; increases real debt burdens; monetary policy is constrained at the zero lower bound. Arguments against: high inflation erodes savings and creates uncertainty; hyperinflation can destroy a currency; benign deflation from productivity is not harmful. Supported judgement: Persistent demand-led deflation is usually more damaging than moderate inflation, which is why central banks target low positive inflation of about 2%.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hyperinflation"?
options: Inflation measured excluding volatile items such as food and energy prices
The rate of inflation that firms, workers and consumers expect in the future, which influences wage and price setting
An index measuring the average change in the prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by a typical household, weighted by expenditure shares
Extremely rapid inflation, often defined as more than 50% a month
items.answer: Extremely rapid inflation, often defined as more than 50% a month
items.markingKey: D. "hyperinflation" is extremely rapid inflation, often defined as more than 50% a month.

items.stem: Explain why deflation can lead to a deflationary spiral.
items.answer: Falling prices encourage consumers to delay spending and raise the real value of debts; AD falls, firms cut output and wages, which reduces incomes and pushes prices down further.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Falling prices encourage consumers to delay spending and raise the real value of debts; AD falls, firms cut output and wages, which reduces incomes and pushes prices down further. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between demand-pull inflation and cost-push inflation.
items.answer: Demand-pull inflation comes from AD rising faster than AS (output rises with prices); cost-push inflation comes from higher production costs shifting SRAS left (output falls as prices rise).
items.markingKey: Demand-pull inflation comes from AD rising faster than AS (output rises with prices); cost-push inflation comes from higher production costs shifting SRAS left (output falls as prices rise). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: According to the expectations-augmented Phillips curve, what happens if the government keeps unemployment below the natural rate?
items.answer: Inflation accelerates as expectations adjust upwards
items.markingKey: Inflation accelerates as expectations adjust upwards. LRPC is vertical at the NRU.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "The Phillips curve shows that governments can permanently reduce unemployment by accepting higher inflation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The expectations-augmented model shows that the trade-off is only short-run; in the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate with higher inflation.
items.markingKey: The expectations-augmented model shows that the trade-off is only short-run; in the long run unemployment returns to the natural rate with higher inflation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that the Phillips curve shows that governments can permanently reduce unemployment by accepting higher inflation. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.stem: With reference to stagflation in the USA in the 1970s, explain how it illustrates shifts of the short-run Phillips curve.
items.answer: US inflation exceeded 13% in 1980 while unemployment rose above 7%, contradicting the stable trade-off suggested by the original Phillips curve. Oil shocks and rising expectations shifted the SRPC outwards, so inflation and unemployment rose together
items.markingKey: Context (US inflation exceeded 13% in 1980 while unemployment rose above 7%, contradicting the stable trade-off suggested by the original Phillips curve.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Oil shocks and rising expectations shifted the SRPC outwards, so inflation and unemployment rose together – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to shifts of the short-run Phillips curve.

items.stem: Elena writes: "A movement along the SRPC is caused by a supply shock." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Movements along the SRPC are caused by changes in AD; supply shocks and changes in expectations shift the SRPC.
items.markingKey: Movements along the SRPC are caused by changes in AD; supply shocks and changes in expectations shift the SRPC. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that there is no trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
items.answer: There is a short-run trade-off but no stable long-run trade-off; policy can only lower unemployment permanently by reducing the NRU.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: vertical LRPC once expectations adjust; 1970s stagflation; credible central banks anchor expectations. Arguments against: short-run trade-off clearly exists; post-2021 inflation rose as labour markets tightened; hysteresis may make the NRU depend on past unemployment. Supported judgement: There is a short-run trade-off but no stable long-run trade-off; policy can only lower unemployment permanently by reducing the NRU.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Simultaneously high inflation and high unemployment, shown by an outward shift of the SRPC"?
options: macroeconomic objectives
stagflation
wage-price spiral
trade-off
items.answer: stagflation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of stagflation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the short-run Phillips curve and the long-run Phillips curve.
items.answer: The SRPC shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment for given expectations; the LRPC is vertical at the NRU, showing no trade-off once expectations adjust.
items.markingKey: The SRPC shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment for given expectations; the LRPC is vertical at the NRU, showing no trade-off once expectations adjust. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the long-run Phillips curve and the natural rate of unemployment, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Vertical LRPC at the NRU; a series of SRPCs for different expected inflation rates; attempts to keep unemployment below the NRU cause accelerating inflation as expectations adjust.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Vertical LRPC at the NRU; a series of SRPCs for different expected inflation rates; attempts to keep unemployment below the NRU cause accelerating inflation as expectations adjust. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Raising interest rates to reduce inflation is likely to conflict with which objective?
items.answer: Low unemployment
items.markingKey: Low unemployment. Higher rates reduce AD and employment.

items.stem: A student claims that macroeconomic objectives always conflict, so governments must choose only one. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Some objectives are complementary: supply-side growth can reduce unemployment and inflation together; conflicts are mainly short-run trade-offs.
items.markingKey: Some objectives are complementary: supply-side growth can reduce unemployment and inflation together; conflicts are mainly short-run trade-offs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the US Federal Reserve's rate rises in 2022-2023 as an example, explain conflict between low inflation and growth.
items.answer: The Fed raised its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 to 5.25-5.50% by July 2023 to bring down inflation from 9.1%. Higher rates reduced inflation but risked slowing growth and raising unemployment, although the labour market stayed strong
items.markingKey: Context (The Fed raised its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 to 5.25-5.50% by July 2023 to bring down inflation from 9.1%.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to the Bank of England's dilemma in 2022-2023, explain how it illustrates conflicts between macroeconomic objectives.
items.answer: In 2022-23 the Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 0.1% to 5.25% while the UK economy was close to recession. Tightening to cut inflation from 11.1% risked higher unemployment and slower growth
items.markingKey: Context (In 2022-23 the Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 0.1% to 5.25% while the UK economy was close to recession.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Tightening to cut inflation from 11.1% risked higher unemployment and slower growth – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to conflicts between macroeconomic objectives.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that low inflation should be the main priority of macroeconomic policy.
items.answer: Low inflation is a necessary foundation, but rigid prioritisation can cause avoidable unemployment; a flexible approach that balances objectives is preferable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: provides stability for investment; protects real incomes of the poor; credible inflation targets anchor expectations. Arguments against: may sacrifice growth and employment in the short run; unemployment has large human costs; sustainability and equity also matter. Supported judgement: Low inflation is a necessary foundation, but rigid prioritisation can cause avoidable unemployment; a flexible approach that balances objectives is preferable.

items.stem: Explain why economic growth may worsen the current account balance.
items.answer: Higher incomes raise spending on imports, and if domestic demand grows faster than exports, the current account deficit widens.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher incomes raise spending on imports, and if domestic demand grows faster than exports, the current account deficit widens. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: An economy has inflation of 6% and unemployment of 3.5%, below its estimated natural rate of 4.5%. Identify which macroeconomic objective is not being met and explain one policy conflict the central bank faces.
items.answer: Low and stable inflation is not being met (6% above a typical 2% target). Raising interest rates would reduce inflation but lower AD, raising unemployment towards (or above) the NRU and slowing growth.
items.markingKey: Low and stable inflation is not being met (6% above a typical 2% target). Raising interest rates would reduce inflation but lower AD, raising unemployment towards (or above) the NRU and slowing growth.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "deflation".
items.answer: A sustained fall in the general price level (negative inflation)

items.stem: Which of the following is most likely to cause demand-pull inflation?
options: A rise in world oil prices
A large rise in government spending when the economy is near full employment
Higher wage costs
A drought that reduces harvests
items.answer: A large rise in government spending when the economy is near full employment
items.markingKey: B. Excess demand at full capacity.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "inflationary expectations"?

A process in which rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, which raise firms' costs and lead to further price rises
The rate of inflation that firms, workers and consumers expect in the future, which influences wage and price setting
An index of the prices of inputs and outputs of producers, often a leading indicator of consumer price inflation
items.answer: The rate of inflation that firms, workers and consumers expect in the future, which influences wage and price setting
items.markingKey: C. "inflationary expectations" is the rate of inflation that firms, workers and consumers expect in the future, which influences wage and price setting.

items.stem: Briefly explain why economic growth may conflict with an equitable distribution of income.

items.stem: Using the "flat" Phillips curve of the 2010s as an example, explain the Phillips curve and anchored expectations.
items.answer: In the late 2010s US unemployment fell to around 3.5% while inflation stayed close to 2%. Credible inflation targeting anchored expectations, so falling unemployment caused only a small rise in inflation
items.markingKey: Context (In the late 2010s US unemployment fell to around 3.5% while inflation stayed close to 2%.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A government wants faster growth and a smaller current account deficit. Explain why expansionary fiscal policy might make one objective harder to achieve, and suggest a policy that could help both.
items.answer: Higher AD raises incomes and import spending, worsening the current account. Supply-side policies that raise productivity and export competitiveness can support growth and improve the current account.
items.markingKey: Higher AD raises incomes and import spending, worsening the current account. Supply-side policies that raise productivity and export competitiveness can support growth and improve the current account.

items.stem: The statistics office of Estoria compiles its CPI from four groups. This year: rent: weight 30%, price index 112; food: weight 35%, price index 110; fuel: weight 20%, price index 112; health care: weight 15%, price index 115. Calculate the weighted price index and the inflation rate since the base year.
items.answer: Weighted CPI = 111.8; inflation since base year = 11.8%
items.markingKey: CPI = Σ(weight × index)/Σweights = 30×112 + 35×110 + 20×112 + 15×115 ÷ 100 = 111.8. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for 111.8. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate cost-push inflation, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2; the price level rises and real GDP falls; caused by rising wages, energy or import prices.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: SRAS shifts left from SRAS1 to SRAS2; the price level rises and real GDP falls; caused by rising wages, energy or import prices. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: "A movement along the SRPC is caused by a supply shock." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Movements along the SRPC are caused by changes in AD; supply shocks and changes in expectations shift the SRPC.
items.markingKey: Movements along the SRPC are caused by changes in AD; supply shocks and changes in expectations shift the SRPC. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Macroeconomic objectives always conflict, so governments must choose only one." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Some objectives are complementary: supply-side growth can reduce unemployment and inflation together; conflicts are mainly short-run trade-offs.
items.markingKey: Some objectives are complementary: supply-side growth can reduce unemployment and inflation together; conflicts are mainly short-run trade-offs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the consumer price index is an accurate measure of changes in the cost of living.
items.answer: It is a reasonable measure of average price changes, but it is less accurate for specific groups and during rapid structural change.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: based on large, regular price surveys; weights updated with expenditure surveys; internationally comparable methodology. Arguments against: substitution, quality and new-product biases; average household may not represent any real household; excludes or poorly measures housing costs in some countries; informal markets omitted. Supported judgement: It is a reasonable measure of average price changes, but it is less accurate for specific groups and during rapid structural change.

items.stem: You are an economist at the trade ministry. A minister argues that deflation is more harmful to an economy than inflation. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Persistent demand-led deflation is usually more damaging than moderate inflation, which is why central banks target low positive inflation of about 2%.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: deflationary spiral reduces AD and output; increases real debt burdens; monetary policy is constrained at the zero lower bound. Counter-points: high inflation erodes savings and creates uncertainty; hyperinflation can destroy a currency; benign deflation from productivity is not harmful. Recommendation: Persistent demand-led deflation is usually more damaging than moderate inflation, which is why central banks target low positive inflation of about 2%. Level 3 (6-8) recommendation supported but justification partly developed. Level 2 (3-5) limited justification. Level 1 (1-2) recommendation asserted.

items.stem:
Read the extract below.

In the late 2010s US unemployment fell to around 3.5% while inflation stayed close to 2%.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that there is no trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
items.answer: There is a short-run trade-off but no stable long-run trade-off; policy can only lower unemployment permanently by reducing the NRU.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: vertical LRPC once expectations adjust; 1970s stagflation; credible central banks anchor expectations. Arguments against: short-run trade-off clearly exists; post-2021 inflation rose as labour markets tightened; hysteresis may make the NRU depend on past unemployment. Judgement: There is a short-run trade-off but no stable long-run trade-off; policy can only lower unemployment permanently by reducing the NRU. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem:
Read the extract below.

The Fed raised its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 to 5.25-5.50% by July 2023 to bring down inflation from 9.1%.

China became the world's largest emitter of CO₂, accounting for around 30% of global emissions, during decades of rapid industrial growth.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that low inflation should be the main priority of macroeconomic policy.
items.answer: Low inflation is a necessary foundation, but rigid prioritisation can cause avoidable unemployment; a flexible approach that balances objectives is preferable.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A fall in the rate of inflation, while prices are still rising"?
options: inflationary expectations
consumer price index (CPI)
disinflation
trade-off
items.answer: disinflation
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of disinflation.

items.stem: Why can deflation be harmful?
options: It increases the real value of savings
It reduces the real value of debt
It makes exports less competitive
Consumers delay purchases expecting lower prices, reducing AD
items.answer: Consumers delay purchases expecting lower prices, reducing AD
items.markingKey: D. Delayed spending and rising real debt burdens.

items.stem: A negative supply shock causes the short-run Phillips curve to:
items.answer: shift outwards (upwards to the right)
items.markingKey: shift outwards (upwards to the right). Higher inflation at every unemployment rate.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a long-run policy conflict and a short-run policy conflict.
items.answer: Short-run conflicts arise mainly from demand management (e.g. the SRPC trade-off); in the long run supply-side improvements can achieve growth with low inflation, but conflicts with sustainability and equity may persist.
items.markingKey: Short-run conflicts arise mainly from demand management (e.g. the SRPC trade-off); in the long run supply-side improvements can achieve growth with low inflation, but conflicts with sustainability and equity may persist. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between headline inflation and core inflation.
items.answer: Headline inflation covers the whole CPI basket; core inflation excludes volatile items such as food and energy to show the underlying trend.
items.markingKey: Headline inflation covers the whole CPI basket; core inflation excludes volatile items such as food and energy to show the underlying trend. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a depreciation of the currency can cause cost-push inflation.
items.answer: Imported raw materials, components and energy become more expensive in domestic currency, raising costs of production, shifting SRAS left and raising the price level.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Imported raw materials, components and energy become more expensive in domestic currency, raising costs of production, shifting SRAS left and raising the price level. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the short-run Phillips curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: When AD rises, firms expand output and hire more workers, reducing unemployment; tighter labour and product markets push up wages and prices, so lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When AD rises, firms expand output and hire more workers, reducing unemployment; tighter labour and product markets push up wages and prices, so lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation. items.stem: "If inflation falls from 6% to 3%, prices are falling." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Prices are still rising, but more slowly (disinflation). Prices fall only with negative inflation (deflation).
items.markingKey: Prices are still rising, but more slowly (disinflation). Prices fall only with negative inflation (deflation). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Euro-area inflation reached 10.6% in October 2022, with energy prices up over 40% year on year. Higher energy costs shifted SRAS left, raising prices while growth slowed

items.stem: Using Argentina's inflation in 2023 as an example, explain measuring inflation.
items.answer: Annual inflation in Argentina exceeded 200% by the end of 2023. Rapid price changes required frequent price collection and reduced the usefulness of fixed-weight baskets

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline demand-pull inflation.
items.answer: AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2 along an upward-sloping SRAS (or towards the vertical section of the Keynesian AS); the price level rises from P1 to P2; caused by rising C, I, G or X.

items.stem: A basket has three items: food (weight 50, price index 112), energy (weight 20, index 140) and services (weight 30, index 104). Calculate the CPI, then explain how the inflation rate experienced by a low-income household spending 70% on food and energy would differ.
items.answer: CPI = (50×112 + 20×140 + 30×104)/100 = 115.2 (15.2% inflation). A low-income household with heavier weights on food and energy faces higher inflation, since those indices rose fastest.
